title: I Gave My 11-Year-Old Son $50 for the School Fair, Then His Teacher Called Me in Tears
fb_text:
I gave my eleven-year-old son $50 and told him he could spend it however he liked at the school fair. Before the school day was over, his teacher called me, crying, and said, "Please come here as quickly as possible. You need to see what he did with that money."

Gavin was eleven, and for years it had been just the two of us.

He was the kind of boy who still hugged me before school every morning, then immediately glanced around to see whether any of his friends had noticed.

We had dinner together every evening, sharing the best and worst moments of our day. Most of the time, Gavin bent the rules and told me about two good things instead.

"That's not how the game works."

"You're the mom. You can change the rules."

I couldn't help laughing. "Nice try."

For two weeks, he had talked about nothing but the school fair.

"They're going to have pizza, games, prizes, and enormous cookies, Mom. Like, seriously enormous cookies."

"That sounds like a very important academic experience."

"It is. Extremely important."

The evening before the fair, I found him sitting on his bedroom floor, carefully counting the twelve dollars he had saved.

I pulled a fifty-dollar bill from my wallet. His eyes grew wide.

"Seriously?"

"It's for you."

"The whole fifty?"

"Every dollar. Spend it on whatever you want."

He looked at the bill, then back at me. "What if I waste it on something ridiculous?"

"Then you'll have learned a fifty-dollar lesson."

"You're the best mom ever."

"I'm also the only mom you've got."

"Doesn't make it any less true."

The next morning, he tucked the bill safely into his backpack. As he climbed out of the car, I called after him, "Don't blow the entire thing on cookies!"

He turned around with a huge grin. "No promises!"

I watched him hurry toward the school entrance, and the money completely slipped my mind.

That was until 2:18 that afternoon, when my phone rang.

It was Gavin's teacher.

"Ms. Madison?"

The moment I heard her voice, I straightened in my seat. "Yes? Is Gavin all right?"

"He's okay."

Then her voice cracked. She was crying.

My heart began to pound. "What happened?"

"I'm sorry. I just... I never expected something like this. Gavin brought fifty dollars to school today, didn't he?"

"Yes."

There was a long pause.

"Please come as quickly as you can. You really need to see what he did with the money."

Twenty minutes later, I hurried through the school entrance. His teacher was standing outside the gym, wiping tears from her face.

"Where is Gavin?"

She gestured toward the doors. "Inside."

And the second I stepped through them, my stomach sank.

"Doesn't make it any less true."

The Phone Call

That was until 2:18 that afternoon, when my phone started ringing. It was Gavin's teacher.

"Ms. Madison?"

The moment I heard her voice, I straightened in my seat. "Yes? Is Gavin all right?"

"He's okay."

Then her voice cracked. She was crying.

"What happened?"

"I'm sorry. I just... I never expected something like this. Gavin brought fifty dollars to school today, didn't he?"

"Yes."

There was another long pause. "Please come as quickly as you can. You really need to see what he did with the money."

Twenty minutes later, I hurried through the school entrance. His teacher was standing outside the gym, wiping tears from her face.

"Where is Gavin?"

She gestured toward the doors. "Inside."

And the second I stepped through them, my stomach sank.

What I Saw in the Gym

Gavin was standing at the ticket table, surrounded by a group of kids. Some of them I recognized from his class. Others I had never seen before. None of them were holding tickets of their own. A few had been standing near the wall earlier, his teacher told me, watching the fair from a distance because they had no money to join in.

My stomach sank because I thought something had gone wrong. But as I stepped closer, I saw that Gavin was handing out tickets, one after another, and the kids around him were laughing, holding paper plates of pizza and, yes, enormous cookies.

He looked up and saw me. His face turned red.

"Mom. You're here."

"Your teacher called me."

"I told her not to make it a big deal."

His teacher stepped up beside me, her voice still shaky. "He came to me before the fair opened. He asked if he could use his money to pay for the kids who couldn't afford to come in. He said he didn't want anyone standing on the sidelines."

I looked at my son. "All fifty dollars?"

He shrugged, suddenly very interested in his shoes. "You said I could spend it on whatever I wanted."

"I did."

"So this is what I wanted."

I felt my eyes fill with tears. A little boy near us, holding a cookie almost as big as his face, looked up at Gavin and said quietly, "Thanks for letting me play."

Gavin just nodded. "Anytime."

A Lesson Worth More Than Fifty Dollars

I pulled him into a hug, right there in the middle of the gym, in front of everyone. For the first time in a long while, he didn't check to see who was watching.

"You're not mad?" he whispered.

"Mad? Gavin, I have never been prouder of anyone in my life."

He pulled back and grinned. "I still had my own twelve dollars. I bought one cookie for myself."

"Was it enormous?"

"Seriously enormous."

That night at dinner, we played our game the way we always do. I asked for the best and worst moments of his day.

"Worst," he said, thinking hard, "that I couldn't find anything bad."

"And the best?"

He smiled. "Can I tell you two good things?"

I laughed, wiped my eyes, and said, "Today, you can break every rule you want."

I told him he had learned a fifty-dollar lesson. But sitting across from him, I realized the lesson had been mine. I had given him the freedom to spend it however he liked, and he showed me exactly who he is.
